lessons.title: Conveying equipment in a feed mill
lessons.html:
Conveying equipment in a feed mill

A feed mill moves thousands of tonnes of grain, meals, minerals and finished feed every month. Most of this movement is done by fixed conveying equipment. As an operator you must know what each machine does, how it fails and how to work near it safely.

Main types of conveyors

EquipmentHow it worksTypical use
Screw (auger) conveyorA rotating spiral pushes material along a trough or tubeShort runs, feeding bins, dosing
Chain (drag/en-masse) conveyorPaddles on a chain drag material along a closed casingHorizontal runs from intake to silos
Belt conveyorA rubber belt on idlers carries materialLong runs, gentle handling, bagged goods
Bucket elevatorBuckets on a belt lift material verticallyRaising grain to the top of silos and bins
Pneumatic conveyingAir moves fine material through pipesMicro-ingredients, dust return

Supporting equipment

  • Distributors and diverter valves send material to the correct bin. A wrong setting means the wrong ingredient in the wrong bin, which is a serious quality failure.
  • Slide gates open and close bin outlets.
  • Magnets catch tramp metal before it damages hammer mills or pellet dies.
  • Scalpers and sieves remove sticks, stones and string.
  • Level sensors stop overfilling and choking.

Common faults

  • Chokes in elevators or screws from overfeeding or wet material.
  • Belt slip, misalignment and worn buckets.
  • Worn chain paddles and sprockets.
  • Blocked spouts and leaking gates causing cross-contamination.

Most faults show early signs: unusual noise, heat, vibration, smell of burning rubber, or a motor drawing high current. Report these signs before they become breakdowns or fires.

lessons.title: Mobile equipment, safety and care
lessons.html:
Mobile equipment, safety and care

Mobile handling equipment

  • Forklifts: move pallets of bagged ingredients, premixes and finished feed.
  • Pallet jacks: short moves on level floors.
  • Front-end loaders and skid steers: handle bulk material on floors and in bunkers.
  • Bag stitchers and palletisers: close bags and stack them on pallets.

Regulations under the Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 require that lift truck and similar machine operators are trained and authorised by the employer. Never drive a forklift unless you hold that authorisation.

Safe use of a forklift

  1. Do a pre-use check: tyres, forks, chains, hydraulics, brakes, hooter, lights and seat belt. Record it on the checklist.
  2. Do not exceed the rated load on the load plate.
  3. Travel with forks low and the mast tilted back.
  4. Drive slowly, look in the direction of travel and use the hooter at corners.
  5. Never lift people on forks.
  6. Park with forks on the floor, engine off and key removed.

Fixed equipment safety

  • Lockout: before clearing a choke, opening an inspection door or changing a screen, isolate the motor, lock it out with your own lock and tag, and test that it will not start.
  • Guards stay on drives, couplings and chains. Report missing guards.
  • Dust: grain and feed dust can explode in elevators and enclosed spaces. Keep housekeeping good, keep dust collection working, and never use open flames or grinders without a hot-work permit.
  • Confined spaces: bins, pits and silos are entered only under a permit with a standby person.

Basic care

  • Follow the lubrication schedule.
  • Check belt tension and alignment.
  • Clean magnets every shift and record what is found.
  • Report wear early so maintenance can plan repairs.

Key points

  • Screws, chains, belts, elevators and pneumatic systems each suit different jobs.
  • Wrong diverter settings cause cross-contamination; always check routing.
  • Lock out and test before any work on fixed equipment.
  • Only authorised operators may drive forklifts.
  • Grain dust is explosive; control dust and ignition sources.
